NIST's fifth post-quantum standard, selected March 2025 as a code-based backup to ML-KEM specifically because it rests on different math -- so one break can't take both down.

A controlled gate applied to a target already in one of its eigenstates leaves the target untouched and dumps the eigenvalue's phase onto the control instead -- the mechanism inside Deutsch-Jozsa, Grover's and phase estimation alike.
Random restart, simulated annealing and oscillator relaxation race on the same graph, 200 replays each -- move the time budget and the winner changes.

A physical network -- built from coupled oscillators or lasers -- engineered so its own resting state solves an optimisation problem. The classical rival every quantum annealer actually competes against.
A unit that keeps fluctuating between 0 and 1 instead of settling, with the odds of each set by its neighbours -- a physical Boltzmann machine, now demonstrated at a million-unit scale.
Treating a circuit's own electrical noise as the computational resource -- for sampling, Bayesian inference and diffusion models -- rather than something to engineer away.
A coil and a capacitor trading energy back and forth at one fixed rate -- the harmless-looking oscillator that turns out to be useless as a qubit on its own.
How unevenly spaced a circuit's energy levels are -- zero for a plain LC tank, and the one property a superconducting qubit cannot work without.
Two superconductors separated by a gap thin enough to tunnel through -- the one component in the circuit that isn't a straight line, which is the entire trick.
A capacitor wired across a single Josephson junction -- the most common superconducting qubit design, and almost the same circuit as a plain LC tank with one piece swapped.
A resonant drive swinging a qubit's population between two levels -- stop it exactly halfway (a pi-pulse) and you have physically performed an X gate.
Spreading one fragile qubit across many so the machine can find mistakes without ever looking at the answer.
The error-correcting code almost every hardware roadmap is built on -- a grid where only neighbours are ever compared.
The alarm pattern a code emits. It says whether neighbours disagree, never what they are -- which is why measuring it does not destroy the data.
The algebra underneath every surface code: operators the encoded state is required to be a +1 eigenstate of.
The proof that arbitrarily long fault-tolerant computation is possible at all, provided the physical error rate sits below a fixed constant and the code scales up to compensate.
Clifford gates alone are classically simulable, so universality is smuggled in via a purified magic state -- consume several noisy copies, distill out fewer higher-fidelity ones.
A gate applied to every physical qubit of a logical block independently, so one faulty gate can't spread -- but Eastin-Knill proves no code can make a gate set both transversal and universal.
Executing a logical two-qubit gate by physically merging adjacent surface-code patches and measuring the joint stabilizers, instead of needing two patches' qubits to sit side by side.
The software that reads the alarms and guesses what actually went wrong. This is the seat AI is currently taking.
The standard hand-written decoder: pair up the alarms using the cheapest explanation. Optimal under uniform noise, and only under uniform noise.
How many single failures a code can absorb before the logical bit flips. Raising it by two buys one more power of suppression; raising an odd d by one buys nothing.
One reliable qubit built out of many unreliable ones. The only qubit count that means anything.
The actual hardware qubit. Thousands of them may be spent to make a single logical one.
The line the whole field is racing to stay under. Below it, more qubits compound into reliability; above it, more qubits make things worse.
How much the error rate falls per two steps of code distance. Google's Willow measured 2.14 for the d=5 to d=7 step.
A qubit holding a definite state that is not one of the answers you can read out.
Correlations two particles share that no classical strategy can fake -- and which still cannot carry a message.
The experiment that proves entanglement is real: play it and watch the win rate cross a ceiling classical physics cannot pass.
One qubit drawn as a point on a sphere. Six real gates rotate it live.
The class of problems a quantum computer solves efficiently. None of its containments is proven strict.
Why exponential state space is not the reason quantum computers are hard to simulate -- stabilizer circuits have it too and simulate efficiently.
The algorithm that breaks RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, given a large enough error-corrected machine.
Quantum search: a quadratic speedup, not an exponential one -- and one step too many makes it worse.
The signature scheme protecting Bitcoin -- and the one Shor's algorithm actually targets.
Cryptography designed to survive a quantum computer -- already standardised, already deployable, and not free on the wire.
The standardised post-quantum key exchange. Bigger than what it replaces, and that size has a measurable cost.
The standardised post-quantum signature scheme.
The conservative hash-based signature. Its real cost is not the 7,856-byte signature -- it is the seconds it takes to produce one.
Traffic recorded today, decrypted whenever a quantum computer arrives. It is why key exchange is urgent and signatures are not.
The one-line test for whether you are already late: secrecy lifetime plus migration time against time-to-quantum.
A machine big enough to break real cryptography. Nobody knows the date, so the honest treatment is a probability curve, not a year.
A machine-readable list of every algorithm in your estate. Paste certificates and the page decodes the ASN.1 itself.
The NSA's post-quantum timetable. Not one date: software signing and networking are 2030, not 2033.
Running a classical and a post-quantum key exchange together, so breaking one is not enough.
The most-claimed and least-shown application. The honest near-term win is quantum-grown data, not faster training.
The exponential-speedup headline that dies on its own fine print: sparsity, conditioning, and getting the answer out.
Gradients that vanish exponentially with qubit count, so the variational circuit has nothing to descend.
Classical algorithms that matched several claimed quantum speedups once the same data assumptions were granted.
The toll that kills most quantum-ML speedups: getting classical data into the machine costs what the speedup saved.
SymbiQ's whole thesis in one diagram: one direction is shipping now, the other is mostly ahead.
Fast gates, short coherence, fabrication that scales like chips. Google and IBM's bet.
Long coherence and all-to-all connectivity, paid for in gate speed.
Optical tweezers holding thousands of identical atoms, with rearrangeable geometry.
Room temperature and natural networking, fighting loss as the central enemy.
How long a qubit holds its state before the environment scrambles it -- T1 is the fall back to |0>, T2 the shorter time for phase to wash out.
The metric that actually beats qubit count when you are reading a hardware announcement.
The field that already decides your delivery route, your shift roster and your power grid -- and the classical baseline quantum optimisation has to beat.
Why you can skip infinitely many points and only check the corners.
Every optimisation problem has a shadow twin that tells you where the next rupee should go.
Why demanding whole numbers turns an easy problem hard.
How to search a space too big to search, by proving whole regions cannot contain the answer.
How much you can push through a network -- and the bottleneck that answers the same question backwards.
Pairing things up without being greedy. The same algorithm runs inside a quantum decoder.
Why the direct road is not the fastest route, and how optimal tails make the search tractable.
Why systems collapse well before they are full.
What you do when proof is out of reach and you still need a good answer today.
The outcome nobody can improve on alone -- even when everyone would rather be somewhere else together.
Why bluffing only works if it's genuinely random -- and why solving it is a linear program in disguise.
The one fair way to split credit a group earned together -- proven unique in 1953, now explaining ML predictions.
Designing the rules of a game so that honesty becomes the winning move.
What happens when strategies spread by succeeding, not by being reasoned about -- from animal contests to cancer treatment.
How you actually find the best corner once you know the optimum is one: walk the edges of the feasible region, only ever uphill, until no neighbour scores higher.
The relaxation that turns a hard combinatorial problem into unit vectors on a sphere -- and the actual classical benchmark quantum optimisation has to beat.
A flow network with no interior -- supply nodes and demand nodes only -- so the optimum sits at a vertex before you even start solving.
Ask whether a solution exists at all before asking which is best -- map-colouring and Sudoku are the same problem underneath.
The encoding every quantum optimisation claim rests on: turn your problem into a magnet and find its ground state.
Hot early to cross ridges, cold late to settle. Play the cooling schedule, not the climber.
The NP-hard problem that is the standard proving ground for quantum optimisation.
Reach a target state in as few gates as possible. Every par is a proven minimum.
Sit in the AI's chair and out-decode minimum-weight matching on a chip with a defect it cannot express.
Six acts where the character's flaw is the mechanic, and the physics does the judging.
One question at a time, at three depths, with a fault-tolerant streak.
Every mistake we have made, run louder than the original claim.
The quantum bit: the unit everything else is counted in.
Computing reliably out of unreliable parts -- the regime the whole roadmap is aimed at.
The four rules everything else in quantum computing follows from: state, evolution, measurement, composite systems.
The object that honestly describes a qubit entangled with something you can't see -- genuinely mixed, not just uncertain.
The general form of quantum measurement -- and the reason two non-orthogonal states can never be told apart for certain.
A four-line proof that no machine can copy an unknown quantum state -- the reason QEC can't just keep a backup.
Moving an unknown qubit's state using a shared entangled pair and two classical bits -- no quantum channel, no cloning, no faster-than-light signal.
Sending two classical bits by physically transmitting just one qubit, spending a pre-shared entangled pair -- teleportation's mirror image.
The one basis pair in which any two-part quantum state collapses to a short matched list -- the honest, basis-independent measure of how entangled it is.
One query settles whether a 1-bit function is constant or balanced, where a classical algorithm needs two -- the first proof of phase kickback plus interference.
One query beats an exponential classical worst case for the same constant-or-balanced promise, scaled to n bits -- an oracle separation, proven exactly.
Finds a function's secret XOR-period in O(n) queries against a classical birthday-bound floor of about root-2^n -- the direct forerunner of Shor's period-finding.
The classical discrete Fourier transform applied to a quantum superposition's amplitudes -- built from O(n^2) gates, exponentially fewer than the classical FFT needs.
Reads out a unitary's eigenvalue to t bits of precision using t counting qubits, controlled powers of the unitary, and an inverse QFT.
Turns phase estimation's measured decimal back into the exact period Shor's algorithm needs -- and, when the measured numerator shares a factor with the period, only a divisor of it, provably.

The same hybrid quantum-classical loop -- a tunable circuit, measured, adjusted by a classical optimizer -- pointed at a graph's cost Hamiltonian (QAOA) or a molecule's (VQE); neither has a proven speedup over its best classical rival.

Chopping time into many small steps to approximate the evolution of a Hamiltonian whose terms don't commute -- the mechanical trick that turns Feynman's 1982 intuition into Lloyd's 1996 algorithm, and the route from a molecule's Hamiltonian to its ground-state energy.
The expected number of bits needed to resolve a random outcome -- zero for a sure thing, log2(n) at most, achieved only by a uniform distribution over n outcomes.

Shannon entropy applied to a density matrix's eigenvalues -- zero for any pure state, yet a pure whole can split into two individually maximally-uncertain halves, the number that quantifies entanglement itself.
The Bellman equation once the world stops guaranteeing your action lands where you aimed it -- and what changes when nobody hands you the transition probabilities at all.

A single electron or nuclear spin in a silicon quantum dot as the qubit -- betting the entire existing chip-fabrication industry instead of building bespoke hardware, and already past 99% fidelity in a real 300mm foundry.

A bet that braided Majorana zero modes protect quantum information by topology alone, before any error correction runs -- and, as of Microsoft's disputed 2025 Majorana 1 announcement, still an unresolved experimental claim, not a settled one.

Uses quantum measurement disturbance (BB84, B92) or Bell-inequality violation (Ekert91) to let two parties detect an eavesdropper directly -- real physics, flown on China's Micius satellite, and not a substitute for the classical/post-quantum cryptography this page's tools actually measure.

Physical hardware that deforms a system toward a problem's Ising-model ground state instead of applying gates -- real and commercially built by D-Wave since 2011, but solves exactly one problem shape and is not a universal quantum computer.

Compute by measuring a fixed, pre-entangled cluster state one qubit at a time, adapting each basis choice to earlier outcomes -- no gate ever applied after the state is built, and the model closest to how a photonic machine actually wants to compute.

Encodes information in a continuous quantity -- a light mode's amplitude and phase -- instead of a discrete qubit; the architecture behind both Jiuzhang's and Xanadu Borealis's headline photonic advantage claims.

The chain-of-purified-hops fix for the fact that an unknown quantum state can't be amplified like a classical signal -- proposed in 1998, still mostly lab-scale (a real three-node network exists), and the reason a satellite sidesteps the whole problem for one specific link.

Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum, the era the field is actually in -- and the still-unsettled tug-of-war between Google's 2019 Sycamore claim and classical simulations that have matched, lost to, and matched it again since.
The quantum analogue of NP: a claim is true if some quantum witness convinces a fast quantum verifier, false if every witness fails to.
The decision version of finding a Hamiltonian's ground energy -- the formal problem VQE is a heuristic for, and QMA's own natural complete problem.
Kitaev's proof that the local Hamiltonian problem is as hard as anything in QMA, by encoding a quantum circuit's entire computation as one Hamiltonian's ground state.
Relaxing a physical system slowly into a Hamiltonian's ground state -- proven polynomially equivalent in power to the standard quantum circuit model.
The still-open question of whether the local Hamiltonian problem stays QMA-hard even at coarse, constant-fraction precision -- the quantum analogue of the classical PCP theorem.

You configure a calibration agent's per-round behaviour -- Trust, Nudge or Recalibrate -- while a qubit's true detuning drifts out of sight; scored against a paired replay of the same drift under a fixed strategy.
Build a solution by taking whatever looks best right now and never reconsidering -- sometimes provably optimal (matroids, minimum spanning tree), more often provably within a fixed factor of optimal.
A proof, worked out before the algorithm is run, that its answer is always within a fixed factor of the true optimum -- the certificate that separates a trustworthy heuristic from a hopeful one.

Set functions with diminishing returns, where greedy is a guaranteed (1 - 1/e)-approximation and provably nothing polynomial beats it -- the bound under sensor placement, feature selection and influence maximisation.

Deciding now against a probability distribution over what comes later, minimising expected cost with a corrective 'recourse' decision once the uncertainty resolves -- how day-ahead power-grid unit commitment is actually solved.

Optimising the worst case over a set of possible data rather than the average, buying a hard guarantee at a measurable cost in expected performance -- the same instinct as a noise-robust quantum control pulse.

The one-decision stochastic problem: order Q before demand is known, and the optimal Q is the demand quantile at Cu/(Cu+Co) -- the rule behind airline seat protection and inventory safety stock alike.

When goals genuinely conflict, 'optimal' becomes a set -- the Pareto front of non-wasteful trade-offs -- and choosing a point on it is a values call, not a theorem; weighted-sum scalarisation silently misses the non-convex parts.

The oldest formula in operations research (Harris, 1913): order sqrt(2KD/h) at a time to balance ordering cost against holding cost -- with reorder points, safety stock, and the bullwhip effect it scales into across a supply chain.
